BBC, 22 Nov 2026 06:35 GMT

Village referendum 'sent powerful message' now government must listen

94% of villagers who took part in the Barnham referendum voted in protest at plans for asylum seekers to be housed at the local MOD base

A close up of the ballot paper with a cross against the word Yes. The ballot paper reads \"In light of central government's failure to respect local consent.... do you support the petition to the crown requesting that Barnham seeks to become an independent, self governing Crown Dependency\"

Local politicians have called on the government to take notice of a referendum held in the village of Barnham and re-think its plans for housing asylum seekers nearby.

Ninety-four percent of those who took part voted to become independent of the United Kingdom as a way of protesting against a proposal to house migrants at the former RAF Barnham military base.

The police and crime commissioner for Suffolk said the symbolic result \"sends a powerful message\" while the leader of Suffolk County Council warned \"society starts to collapse when politicians stop listening\".

The Home Office says it recognises the strength of feeling and insisted that it is listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

There have been regular protests outside the former military camp ever since the government announced it was considering it for asylum seekers

No-one was surprised by the outcome of the poll which saw 257 people vote for the village ''to become an independent self-governing Crown dependency'' and just 16 vote against the idea.

The result has no legal basis, but there were warnings from local politicians for ministers not to ignore the result.

\"It sends a powerful message that it is a completely unsuitable site.

\"I hope just for once that the government will actually listen to local people,\" said Tim Passmore the Conservative Police and Crime Commissioner for Suffolk.

\"That is what Andy Burnham said he would do, now it's time for action.\"

Terry Jermy is the Labour MP for Thetford, which is just two miles away from the base.

He said: \"The people of Barnham have done a really good job in raising awareness of the issue and demonstrating the strength of feeling against these plans.

\"The message to the government is that this MoD site is not suitable.\"

While Michael Hadwen, the Reform UK leader of Suffolk County council, said: \"This is a clear demonstration of democracy at work.

\"Barnham has said loud and clear that that the government cannot impose this base upon them and the government should start to listen because when things like this start to get ignored that's when society starts to collapse.\"

The estimated turnout of around 70% was lower than campaigners had been hoping for.

When a similar referendum was held in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington 89% of locals took part.

The chair of the residents association in Barnham said some people had decided not to vote after seeing the government ignore the result in Piddington and give planning permission for a nearby military base to be used for asylum seekers.

What's the government's reaction?

A Home Office spokesman said: \"We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

\"The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1 billion saved in costs since the election.

\"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

\"These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.\"

The Home Office also pointed out that whilst it has submitted an application to obtain planning permission to use the Barnham site, it is still assessing the base and no final decisions have been taken on the site's future use.

Members of the Barnham Residents' Association unveil the new image which will become the  flag of Barnham - a protected Stone-curlew

Barnham's Labour MP Peter Prinsley, is due to meet the immigration minister later this week where he says he will draw her attention to the referendum result and express his continued belief that the site is too remote to house asylum seekers.

\"I'm still optimistic the eventual outcome will be that this is not a suitable place,\" he said.

Earlier this month, the government awarded a £3.4m contract to the construction company Kier to assess the viability of the Barnham site and draw up plans for it to accommodate asylum seekers while their applications are processed.

Some campaigners believe that the firm will conclude that the site is inappropriate.

They have suggested that the accommodation blocks could need major renovation and that the sewage and water system may be in need of repair.

They also wonder if the ground around the former nuclear weapons base could be contaminated. No one seems to know the answer to these questions at the moment.

After the referendum result a picture of a Stone-curlew was unveiled as the new image on the village flag. The protected species has been sighted in the area and may present another obstacle to the site being used.

There could also be delays in accessing the site should the government decide to use it.

Suffolk Police has a lease to use the base for training and storage which requires the MoD to give six months notice if it wants to take it back.

Suffolk County Council has also vowed to continue its fight.

\"If the government keeps ignoring us we will look for other means to stop this from happening,\" Hadwen said.

\"And if the government does decide to go ahead I will look at all legal means to stop those gates from being opened.\"

There seems to be a lot of obstacles to overcome and the referendum result appears to have given campaigners added impetus.
